column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article gives 1399 as the start of vassalage to England and 1405 for the Stanley grant; both agree with the entry. Left out the modern-terms equivalents of the sums and the name of the 1825 Act, which the article oddly ties to the 1828 sale.

The entry says the title Lord of the Isles was first used by John of Islay in 1336; the article says the title began with Somerled in the 12th century. The text says only that Somerled founded the dynasty that in time became the Lords of the Isles and gives his own titles, without saying who first used the title. Left out the present holder (Prince William) to keep the text free of present-day statements; the entry already says the heir apparent holds it.

The entry calls Vannius 'of the Quadi'; the article calls him the Roman-installed king of the Suebi. The text does not repeat the Vannius episode, which the entry already gives. The entry dates the sources to the 1st and 2nd centuries CE; the article says the record runs to the 3rd century. The text says only that they vanish in the 3rd century, as the article does, which does not contradict the entry's account of the main sources.

The entry dates his death c. 478; the article's lead gives c. 478 but its body says he died at Troyes in 479 and was bishop for fifty-two years. Neither the year of death nor the length of his episcopate is given. The article's lead says the British bishops asked for help around 426; the body dates the mission to autumn 429, as the entry does. Only the 429 date is used.

The article gives his birth as c. 1910 or 1908 and his death as after 1936; the entry has c. 1910-1937. No birth year is printed; the only death date given is Sheng Shicai's claim of 1937, attributed. Left out Rokossovsky's claim that he was released and fought in the Second World War, and the Who's Who in China error.
The article is short (about 345 words); the text uses nearly all of it. It gives no start date for his rule (the entry has about 211 BCE).
The article's lead says he was chief of the general staff in 1918-20, its body that he took the post on 26 March 1919; no date is given for his appointment.
The article's Economy section describes Maradi, not Madaoua, and was not used.

The entry frames the state through Darfur, 1874-1898 (the Mahdist interregnum there); the article does not mention al-Zubayr or 1874. The text keeps to what the article gives and does not date the start of Mahdist rule in Darfur. The article's lead says remnants held out in Darfur until 1909, after the Anglo-Egyptian reconquest of 1898; the text says the restored sultanate destroyed the last holdout in 1909, which fits the entry's end of the interregnum in 1898.
The article dates the assembling of the squadron for Madras to 1744; the entry says he captured Madras in 1746. The text gives no year for the expedition.

SKIPPED: the article has only two sentences of history beyond the entry; the rest is administration, language counts, schools and a list of sights, one of which (a 12th-century temple called the Stone house) contradicts the entry's Kachari stone house

The article gives his birth as c. 906 and says he lived to 84; the entry has c. 910. No birth year or age is printed. The article says he gave up the abbacy two years before his death and made Odilo his coadjutor; the entry has him abbot from 954 to 994. That point is left out.
The article dates him to the 6th or 5th century BCE; the entry says 5th century BCE. No century is printed; Basham's 484 BCE falls in the 5th.
The article calls the Ottoman commander only Mustafa; the entry names him Lala Mustafa Pasha.
The entry dates his death to 2 CE; the article gives c. 55 BC - after 2 BC. No year of birth or death is printed. The entry spells the tribe Sugambri; the article has Sicambri, used here.
The article says it is unclear when he died, between 1660 and 1662; the entry has around 1661. No year of death is printed.

The article says Mastino abandoned the policy of balance 'held by his father'; his father Alboino was not the ruler before him (Cangrande I was), so the text says 'his predecessors'. The article's marriage line ('Taddea da Carrara (daughter of Jacopo I of Padua) and Anna Gradenigo (daughter of Pietro Gradenigo)') is garbled; Anna Gradenigo is left out. The article does not name Padua or Treviso among the lost cities; the entry's statement is left alone. The article dates the war's end to 1339 as the entry does.

The article gives his reign as 98/85 to 60/57 BCE; the entry has r. c. 85–60 BCE. No reign dates are given in the text. The entry calls him the first major Indo-Scythian king; the article calls him the first Indo-Scythian king. Left as the entry has it.
The article is short and mostly bibliography; two sections only. The entry's command against the Bagaudae and the Forum of Trajan are not in the article and are not repeated.

The entry names his father as Chemosh-yatti; the article says the name is only partly preserved and Chemosh-yat(ti) is the reconstruction with some acceptance. The text gives that, which explains rather than contradicts the entry.
Klein dates the golden age to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabela (so spelt in the article); written as the age before Charles V to avoid the misspelling.

The article says the remains were dug up 'twelve years later' than 331 (343) in one place and gives 342 in the family section; the entry has 342, which the text follows without the 'twelve years' phrase.

The article gives his reign as 515 to 542; the entry dates his death c. 540. No end year is given in the text. The article dates the Battle of Sondani 'between 525 and 532 CE, likely by 530' in the lead and 528 in the Mandsaur section; no year is given in the text.
The article dates the translation of Saint Sava's relics to Mileševa to 1236; the entry says they were kept there from 1237. No year is given for the translation in the text.

The article dates the foundation to 888; the entry has c. 880. No foundation year is given in the text. The article puts the translations of Arabic works under Abbot Arnulf; the entry under Oliba. The text names Arnulf for the translations, as the article does, and Oliba for the library's growth, which both share.
The article gives no height; the entry's 950 metres is left alone. The article says the Latin festivals were held between January and March; the entry calls the festival annual, which agrees.

The article says the dating of the compilation rests on the last hand having written at the earliest at the end of the 11th or beginning of the 12th century, while its lead calls the work tenth-century, as the entry does. The later date is left out.

The entry calls his father Izzat Pasha al-Abid; the article calls him Ahmad Izzat al-Abid. The text uses the article's fuller name, which is the same man. The entry says he resigned as the National Bloc negotiated a treaty with France; the article says he resigned after a free parliament was elected. The text gives the article's reason only, without a date beyond 1936.

The article's lead gives his birth as 1332 (as the entry does) but its Origin section says 18 March 1333; no birth date is given in the text. The article's lead gives his death as 27 April 1362, its Downfall section 25 or 27 April; the text gives no day.

The numbers of Mukhtar's men executed differ between the sources the article cites (Abu Mikhnaf 7,000; al-Waqidi 700 Arabs and all the Persians, then 6,000); the text gives the article's own range of those who surrendered.
The article's lead says he became Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1890; its Career section and the entry say 1892. The text follows 1892.
The article does not mention the Kangra school of painting; the entry's statement is left alone.

The article says the Muktyala Raja donated 'one hundred and ten million GBP in 1952' and 22,000 ha of land; the money figure looks doubtful and is left out. The article gives the height as 124 m from the deepest foundation in its lead and 125 m maximum in its data table; the text gives 124 m from the deepest foundation.
The entry calls her a goddess of love and war; the article (lead and section openings) speaks only of love, with a bow in late depictions. Not contradicted, war left unmentioned.

The article dates the town to 1919 but says the palace annexe for the viceroys was added in 1910 and that the town was popular with viceroys in the early 1900s: it contradicts itself, so the 1910 date and 'early 1900s' are left out. 1919 agrees with the entry's 'early 20th century'.

Last section is short (two sentences, under 40 words) as the guide allows for The place today. The article says the fort is being renovated by the Archaeological Survey of India; left out as a present-tense state.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, nearly all already in the description (nagas, Anavatapta, four pools, Avalokitesvara, Zhou Daguan); too little to add 260 words

The article says Nerik was ruined by the Kaska under Hantili (an Old Kingdom king, 16th century BCE), while the entry dates the Kaska overrunning it to the 15th century BCE; Hantili's name is left out and the ruin is not dated. Hattusili III's recapture is dated c. 1290 BC in the article (Muwatalli's reign), not given a year here.
The article says Nice joined the French Empire in 1861; the entry gives the annexation as 1860. The year is left out ('after Nice passed to France').

The article's lead gives his episcopate as 1542-1546, while the entry says he was driven out after the Schmalkaldic War in 1547 (the article's body: after Luther's death in 1546 and the Battle of Muhlberg in 1547). The end year of his episcopate is left out.
The article's lead ends his first reign in 1338; the entry says 1340. The end year of the first reign is left out.

The article gives the war's cost both as over £2 million and as £1.131 million; the cost is left out. The article's name section says O'Grady counted from 1594 and confederates called it the 'eleven years war'; left out for space.

The entry says he was killed in battle; the article says he took his own life when pinned under his horse in the siege of Kuromaru. Told as the article tells it, in battle, with 'according to the record'; the editor may want to check the entry's wording.
Article says born in 1841 in its body, c. 1841 in its lead; birth year left out (entry has c. 1841).

The article (lead) says Manley 'served as the first and only premier'; the entry says premier 1955 to 1962 'chief minister and then premier'. No conflict. The article's lead says he 'helped to launch' the PNP; the body says co-founded; the entry says founded. Written as co-founded.
The article gives the population both as 2.07 million (government estimate, 2003) and as about 1,000,000; left out. The entry's kingdom of Taqali is not in the article; not mentioned.

The article distinguishes Nyi Roro Kidul from Kanjeng Ratu Kidul (in Kejawen belief the former is the latter's subordinate), while the entry treats Ratu Kidul as another name of the same figure. The distinction is left out so the page does not disagree with itself; some details above (mermaid, claiming bathers, shape-changing) are told in the article of Kanjeng Ratu Kidul.
The article's lead calls him Marquis of Ferrara and Ancona; not used. The article says Dante put him in the Seventh Circle for purchasing Ghisola; I state both facts without the causal link.

The article says the Oenotrians were absorbed into other Italic tribes by the 6th century BC, and elsewhere that they disappeared from the 5th century BC under Lucanian pressure; it also dates their arrival (Elymian migration) to about 1260 BC while saying they lived in the 8th-7th centuries BC. Dates of absorption and the 1260 BC figure left out.
Short article (about 300 words); two sections only. Left out the Bayerischer Rundfunk programme.
Short article (about 350 words). The Boniface letter and Coenred named in the entry are not in the article, so not repeated.

The article says the company ceased trading in 1734 and was wound up in 1737; the entry's dates 1722-1731 are the charter's span (abolished 1731), so both are kept as the article gives them, without contradicting the 1731 abolition.
The article says around 1,000 Linear B tablets were found in 1939; the entry says more than a thousand. The count is left out.

The article says the sources disagree on the relationship: Pabag is called father, stepfather (Agathias, George Syncellus), grandfather or father-in-law (Olbrycht) of Ardashir, and he had a daughter Denag who married Ardashir. The entry calls him Ardashir's father, so the disagreement is left out. Death: article 'between 207 and 210', entry 'd. c. 210'; written as 'a few years after taking Istakhr'.

The article says the Taleju temple was rebuilt by Srinivasa Malla in 1667, the same year it gives for the Krishna Mandir built by Siddhi Narsingh Malla; both kept as given, without naming who rebuilt Taleju.

The article says he was made governor in November 1755 and reached Buenos Aires in April 1756, while its lead and the entry say governor from 1757: the start date is left out. The article also says he defeated the Portuguese near Santa Catarina in February 1779, after his death in December 1778 (self-contradiction): left out. Left out the son born to his mistress in 1779 ('eight months after he returned to Spain', which does not fit his death).

Birth: article 'born either in 1570 or 1585', entry c. 1587: left out. Size of the expedition: article 47 canoes with 70 soldiers, a few clergymen and 1,200 Natives; entry 'some 2,000 people': the people counted are left out. The article's 'Asia' section (travels to Malacca and Baghdad, Narrative of my Journey from India to Italy) seems to belong to a namesake, the Portuguese traveller Pedro Teixeira: left out.
The article gives the 1749 special remainder once as to Algernon's daughter Elizabeth and once as to his son-in-law Sir Hugh Smithson; worded so as not to choose.
The article gives the Byblos tombs as 'from Middle Kingdom times'; the entry says Middle Bronze Age. Not repeated.
The article dates the dictionary to 1773 in its text and 1772 in its list of works: the year is left out.
The article gives 4,150 men surrendered at Paardeberg; the entry says about 4,000. The number is left out.

Birth: article 'before 700', entry c. 670: left out. The article garbles the Reichenau founding ('which had earlier founded'), so only his appointment as abbot in 724 is given; Murbach's date (entry 727) is not in the article.
The article does not mention Savisaar becoming prime minister; the entry's statement is left as it stands.

The article dates the style roughly 1025-900 BCE and says earlier studies put its start around 1050 BCE; the entry gives c. 1050-900 BCE. The text gives neither start year, only the second half of the 11th century for the transition (Toffolo et al. 2013 centre it on about 1025 BCE). The article mentions Knodell's three sub-periods but the excerpt does not give them. Short article: about 270 words.

The article says the British kept a military presence south of the Lakes 'until 1796 and the Jay Treaty' and elsewhere that the posts were turned over after the Jay Treaty (1794); the text gives only the treaty's year. Article says the western districts were detached in 1791 and known as Hesse District until 1792; left vague.

The article's lead gives his reign as 691-716 (matching the entry) but the Reign section says he succeeded his brother in 692; the text gives no accession year. The article does not date the conquest of the Yenisei Kyrgyz (the entry says 710); no year given here. The article dates his Chinese titles to 695 inside the account of 697; left out.

The article gives his birth as between 1009 and 1014 and his death as uncertain: Hedayat says 1072, a qasida to Abu Nasr Mamlan suggests he lived until at least 1088, Taqi says 1092. The entry has c. 1009-after 1072; the text gives no death year. The entry names the Rawadid patron Abu'l-Hayja Wahsudan; the article calls him Abu Mansur Wahsudan. The text says only Wahsudan. The article does not mention the 1042 Tabriz earthquake.
The article lists Shimun XXI Eshai as a notable person of the village without saying he was born there. The exile of the line is stated in the entry, not the article's text.
The article does not mention truffles or the Hundred Years' War by name; it covers the English treaties of 1259 and 1360 and the expulsion of 1440.
The fertility figures are the total fertility rate (lifetime births per woman); the text calls it the birth rate for brevity, as the article's own Belanger passage does.

The article gives his birth as typically c. 1840 (alternatives c. 1835, c. 1842, c. 1845); the entry has c. 1842. No birth year given. The article dates the conquest of Bornu 1892-1894 and the invasion of Bornu proper to summer 1893; the entry says 1893. The defeat of Tahr is not narrated in the excerpt beyond the armies' sizes; the text says only that Rabih overcame it, which the conquest implies. The article does not mention Wadai.

The entry credits Ranjitsinhji with improving roads, railways and the port; the article attributes the modernisation (slum clearance, roads, irrigation, the railway extension) to his administrator Berthon. The text names Berthon without denying the entry. The article dates the shooting accident to 31 August 1915 and the removal of the eye to 2 August, an inconsistency; the text says only August 1915. The entry says he played Tests 1896-1902; the article gives 1893-1904 as the main span of his career and 15 Tests. No Test years given here.

The article says al-Mahdi proclaimed himself Imam in 909; the entry says he was proclaimed caliph there in January 910. The text gives no date for the proclamation. The article implies the Fatimid and Zirid periods reorganised the palace interior; left out for length.

The article gives Reginar's dates as c. 850-916 and his ducal rule as 910-915; the entry says he died in 915. No death year given. The entry says the family held counties in Hainaut and the Hesbaye; the article lists Hainaut only.

The article says the rebuilding was finished in 1845 and that Notre-Dame-en-Saint-Melaine served as pro-cathedral from 1803 to 1844; the entry dates the rebuilding 1787-1844. The text gives no completion year. The entry says the building was rebuilt after the old church collapsed; the article says the west front collapsed in 1490 and that in 1754 the nave and choir were demolished, after a stone fell, before they could collapse. The text tells the article's sequence; the editor may wish to reword the entry. The article does not mention the ducal coronations.

The article's excerpt does not cover the 1956 rising, the executions or the restoration of the 1853 constitution, which stay in the entry only. Article: Lonardi formed the provisional government in Córdoba on 20 September and was sworn in on 23 September; the junta's statement said he would take charge on 22 September. Text gives only the swearing-in date.
The article does not mention the Middle Angles.

The entry spells the agent's name Eli Ayres; the article has Dr. Eli Ayers. The text names neither. The article says he bought the Tellurium mine in 1848 in a paragraph about the 1820s-1830s; left out. Frémont is spelled Fremont in the article; check-more may flag the accent.

The entry says Saadi dedicated the Gulistan to Abu Bakr ibn Sa'd; the article says he dedicated the Bostan and Gulistan to Sa'd I and Sa'd II. The text names no dedicatee. The article lists Abish Khatun as ruling 1263-1284, beyond the entry's 1282 end date; no end year given. The article also says 'Following Sa'd I's death, his brother Zangi took power in 1161', which must mean Sunqur; the text follows the list of atabegs. Kish (1229) is not in the article. Short article: the text is about 290 words.

The lead of the article says the uprising began in February 1904; its own War section and the entry say January (12 January 1904). Followed the entry and the body; the February date is left out. The article dates his death 14 March 1923; the text says only March 1923.

The article says he began the palace 'a year after being elected Governor of Transylvania (1777)', which disagrees with its own governorship date of 6 July 1774; no year is given for the start of building. Left out the claim of a daguerreotype portrait of Brukenthal (he died in 1803, before photography) and the ranking of the school. The article gives the German name of Sâmbăta de Jos as 'Untermühlenderf', apparently a misspelling; only the Romanian name is used.
The bell tower (1592), the 1498 confraternity, the 1539 papal permission and the ship tax are already in the entry; they are mentioned only in passing or not repeated.
The entry gives no dates; the Trojan War date of about 1200 BC is Porphyry's placing and the article's gloss, left out as a date for the man.

The article says the Sangkum was formally dissolved on 18 February 1971 and speaks of Sihanouk's first administration as 1955-1971; the entry dates it 1955-1970 and says it ended with his overthrow in 1970. The 1971 dissolution is left out. The entry's claim that it won every seat from 1955 to 1966 is not in the article; nothing added on seat counts.

SKIPPED: The article has under 200 words of substance (the provinces it covers, the railway lines and a demographic note) and adds almost nothing to the entry, which already says more about its history.

The entry's statement that Sasol was privatised from 1979 is not in the article; nothing is said on privatisation. Left out the article's rankings (largest corporate taxpayer, seventh-largest coal miner), employee and country counts given 'as of 2026', and the company's emission targets. The article says Sasol had operations in 33 countries in one place and 31 in another; neither is used.

The entry's independent judiciary and child-marriage ban are in the entry already; the article also names the child-marriage ban. Gayatri Devi's account that he had missed the Durbar rehearsals is left out.

The article reports the Beloch-Meritt group as dating the Athenian return to 447 BC; the entry gives c. 449-448 BCE, so that year is left out ('some time later'). Left out: the article's 'As of 1997' framing for the lack of evidence on pilgrims.

The entry says Häme Castle was built to hold the region; the article says the chronicle's 'taffwesta borg' was traditionally identified as Häme Castle but that the older Hakoinen Castle is now considered more likely. The castle's identity is left out. The article gives the traditional dating as 1249-1250 in its lead and 1247-1250 for Pipping; the entry says c. 1249. Only 1249 is given as the traditional year.

The article gives his birth as 1689 or 1690; the entry has 1689. No birth year is given in the text. Nabi Bakhsh Baloch disputes the story of his youthful love for Saida Begum; only the marriage after 1713 is told.

The article gives his reign as 1425-1432 in its lead but also says he ascended in TH 836 (1432); its tomb section says that, since the 1432 gravestone is not his, his reign must fall after 1515, perhaps beginning 1521-1524. The entry says early 15th century. All reign dates are left out, as is the post-1515 dating. The article's 'ennoblement of its tutelary mountain' and Sulu burial passage was unclear and is left out.

The article also says the Shatuo fell under the Chagatai Khanate in the Mongol period and received Tatar tribute in 966, which sits oddly with their disappearance before the 12th century; left out. The article says the Tang fief of Jin was granted in 883; the entry says he was rewarded with Hedong, consistent.

The article is short (about 350 words); the text keeps to what it says. It says he died in a local skirmish near the Samur River; the entry says he was killed in battle against the Shirvanshah. Both are consistent.

The article says the coins date to about the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE and the bilinguals to the 3rd and 2nd centuries; consistent with the entry's 5th to 2nd centuries. The article calls it probably closely related to Lydian, Carian and Lycian and part of the Luwian family; the entry says related to Luwian and Lycian. Not restated.
The article spells the builder Sidi Sayyad and Sidi Sa'id; the entry Sidi Saiyyed. Used Sidi Sa'id after the tablet's name.

The article is largely unsourced and speculative (Vedic origins, the Vijaya and Nana Sahib claims, a secret tunnel to Somnath); only the claims are reported, as local tradition. It also contains a paragraph about another Sihor, a Chunval village near Viramgam, which is left out. The entry's Gohil seat from the 13th century and the move to Bhavnagar in 1723 are not in the article.
The entry says the county was named after John Graves Simcoe; the article says Simcoe named it in honour of his father, Captain John Simcoe. The naming is left out.
The article says Simon took 'the battles at Dighomi (1567) and Samadlo (1569)' and was captured at Partskhisi in 1569; all as given.
The article says the last four communities 'correspond to' four districts; written as given. The surname Wan from Talavan is left out.

The article speaks of the Persian bureaucracy of the 12th century while dating the work to the eleventh century; the century of the bureaucracy was left out. The article does not mention the emphasis on standing armies given in the entry's description; nothing written contradicts it. Short article (about 465 words): text kept near 330 words.
The article also records a caid match between Louth and Meath at Slane in 1712 and the hymn tune Slane; left out for length.
The article gives his death as 7 February 1815; the year matches the entry. It calls the 1804 agreement vassalage rather than a protectorate; worded as vassalage, which does not contradict the entry.
The entry calls her rival Henry the Illustrious, the Wettin margrave; the article names him Henry III, Margrave of Meissen. Both refer to the same man.
The article says her two children hold British nationality; the entry says her sons held foreign citizenship. Not repeated here. Thin article (about 340 words); two sections only.

The article's lead dates the Spanish period 1557-1707 and the Austrian 1708-1733, while its section headings give 1557-1708; these period limits were left out. Article lists five towns including Ansedonia, and Porto Longone among the territories; the 1557 exclusion list is quoted as the article gives it.

The article says the town was first named for von Stutterheim, later renamed Dohne, and reverted to its previous name in 1857; the entry says it was founded in 1857. The renaming is told without dates to avoid contradicting the entry. Population of 46,730 given in the article was left out (it appears to be the wider area).

The entry dates the temple and baths from the late first century CE; the article dates the cult head possibly to the late first century and the pediment to the first century. Neither date is printed in a way that contradicts the entry.

The article does not date the Battle of the Colline Gate; the entry's November 82 BCE was not repeated. The article calls the second consul both Scipio Asiaticus and Scipio Asiagenus; the form Scipio Asiaticus was used.

The article says he was probably a member of the Musulamii; the entry states it plainly. Not repeated. The article's account of his death has him impaling himself on the spears; this is compatible with the entry's killed in a surprise attack. Ptolemy of Mauretania's later fate and the annexation of Mauretania in 44 CE were left out.
Kawila's dates (1782-1816) and the 1523 shipment of 60 volumes were left out for length.
Contents placed first so the story of the words comes before its history; the editor may reorder.
Article calls him the most remarkable scholar of the Jonang school; the praise was left out.
Short article (about 350 words); The place today kept to two sentences.
The article dates the marriage to around 855; the entry gives 855 plainly. The year was not repeated.

The article says the Phoenician founding in the 8th century BC was long accepted but has been made less likely by a submerged wall in the Mistras Lagoon, perhaps older than the Phoenician port; this contradicts the entry's description, so neither the founding date nor the doubt was printed. The article dates the abandonment both to the 10th century and to 1070 or shortly after; only the 1070 move, which agrees with the entry, was used.
The article gives his second premiership as 1945 to 4 April 1946; the entry's 1945 to 1946 agrees. Metaxas's dictatorship and the 1939 letter to King George II left out for length.

The article gives his death as 924 in one place and 925 or 924/925 in others; the year was left out (the entry has d. c. 925). The article says John X may in fact have been related to Theodora or Theophylact; not repeated.

The article has slips in its dates: Emperor Gaozong of Tang given as r. 618-626, Li Shi as r. 779-804, and the Jin dynasty as both 226-420 and 266-420; none of these dates was used. The article dates the Secretariat-Chancellery merger variously (early Song, Southern Song, 1129); only the general statement was used.

The article dates Utu-hengal's victory to c. 2050 BC; the entry has r. c. 2120 BCE and 'around 2119 BCE'. No date given in the text. The article spells the town of refuge Dabrum; the entry has Dubrum. The town is left unnamed in the text. The article calls Tirigan the 19th ruler while the list counts 21 kings; both kept as the article gives them.

The article's lead gives his death as 9 November 1630 and its body 5 October 1630 (probably Gregorian against lunar); no day given in the text. The entry dates the Tsu domain to 1608, as does the article; not repeated.

Day dates of birth and death (4 April 1800, 29 September 1860) are in the article in month-first form; left out as the entry gives years only. The family list names a 5th son Ikeda Yoshinari of Tottori, while the Legacy section names Ikeda Yoshinori of Inaba (Tottori); the text uses the Legacy section's form.

The article contradicts itself on dates: 13 May 895-947 in the lead, birth 'in the 10th century' correlated to 23 May 671 in the body, and the departure in 947. No exact dates given in the text. The entry's detail that Tezcatlipoca tricked him into disgrace is not in the article; not touched. The article's long passage presenting the Cortés-as-god belief as fact is set against its own statement that most modern scholars see it as a post-conquest myth; the text follows the latter.
The article lists the duties and the 1770 repeal already given in the entry; not repeated beyond what context needs.

The entry places the site's span at perhaps 900 BCE to about 900 CE; the article says it was founded before 1000 BCE and emerged as a regional centre c. 900-800 BCE, so the founding date is given as the article states and the regional-centre date left vague.
Article's post office dates (1885) differ from the capitol and seat dates but do not contradict the entry; left out.
The article dates the caves to the 2nd or 1st century BCE and the Hathigumpha inscription to the 2nd century BCE; the entry gives the 1st century BCE. No century given in the text.
The article dates his birth 595? with a question mark; left out as the entry gives no birth year.
The article gives his death as 29 October 1033 or 1034; the entry says 1034. No year of death given in the text. The article gives his birth as 975 x 992; the entry c. 992. Left out.
The article's sections after 1954 (repression, the EXMIBAL case) are given only in their openings; the civil-war killings in the entry are not detailed in the excerpt.
The article spells the biblical town both Sokho and Socho; the entry writes Socoh. The text uses the article's forms.

The article gives his birth as 1470 (tradition) or about 1478 (recent biographers); the entry has c. 1470. Left out, as is the article's 'died in his 90s'. The article says he was appointed bishop in 1536, made official in 1537, took office 1538; text says appointed in 1537 as officially made.
